passage:
At the Sri Rama Navami fair in Chaitanya's village, Lalit anna played the harmonium on the temple steps, fingers flying, and the whole crowd clapped along. Chaitanya, nine, forgot all about his cotton candy.
On the walk home he announced to Ammamma, "From tomorrow I will practise harmonium every single day. Like Lalit anna!"
Ammamma's old harmonium sat under a cloth in the storeroom. Next morning Chaitanya dragged it out before brushing his teeth and pumped the bellows till dust flew. He played the same three notes over and over, grinning. After school he played again. After dinner he played on the veranda until the neighbour's dog howled.
"Every day," he told Ammamma, tapping her arm. "You'll see."

qa.q: Where did Lalit anna play the harmonium?
qa.a: On the temple steps at the Sri Rama Navami fair.

qa.q: What made Chaitanya want to practise every day?
qa.a: He admired Lalit anna and was thrilled by the clapping crowd, so excitement made him want to play like him.

qa.q: How could Ammamma help this excitement turn into a lasting habit?
qa.a: She could help Chaitanya choose a short, fixed practice time, so a routine is ready for the days when the thrill wears off.

qa.q: How might Ammamma feel hearing the same three notes all day?
qa.a: Ammamma may be amused and touched to hear her old harmonium played again, while wondering how long the excitement will last.

grounding: Shows a child in a village who admires a harmonium player at a fair and eagerly announces daily practice, carried along by excitement.

passage:
On Saturday, Jana's cousin Camila visited from Lisbon and drew everyone around the kitchen table in Berlin: Oma in her reading glasses, Papa mid-yawn, even the cat. The drawings looked alive. Jana, ten, couldn't stop staring at the moving pencil.
That night she found an empty notebook and wrote on the first page in big letters: JANA'S DRAWING BOOK. ONE DRAWING EVERY DAY.
On Sunday she drew her shoe, her lamp and the view from her window. On Monday she drew on the bus to school and again after homework.
"Look, Mama, I've done six already!" she said, holding up the book with smudgy grey fingers.
Mama smiled. "Every day, hm?"
"Every single day, like Camila," Jana said, already sharpening the pencil.

qa.q: What did Jana write on the first page of her notebook?
qa.a: JANA'S DRAWING BOOK. ONE DRAWING EVERY DAY.

qa.q: What does Jana's 'I've done six already!' show about how she feels?
qa.a: It shows she is proud and excited, eager to draw like Camila.

qa.q: What could Mama do to help the habit last once the excitement fades?
qa.a: Mama could help Jana pick a small daily drawing time and keep the book somewhere easy to reach, so it is simple to continue on duller days.

qa.q: How might Camila feel on hearing that Jana draws every day because of the visit?
qa.a: Camila might feel flattered and happy to have inspired Jana 😊, and could encourage her by drawing together next time.

grounding: Illustrates a child starting a daily drawing habit after admiring a cousin's sketches, with excitement making the new habit feel easy.
